title: II. A Critical Moment
paragraphs: Father Païssy, of course, wasn't wrong to think his "dear boy" would come back. He may well have seen, with real insight, the true meaning of Alyosha's spiritual state. Still, I must honestly admit it would be very hard for me to give a clear account of that strange, hazy moment in the life of the young hero I care about so much. To Father Païssy's sorrowful question, "Are you too among those of little faith?" I could of course answer confidently on Alyosha's behalf, "No, he isn't among those of little faith. Quite the opposite." In fact, all his trouble came from the fact that his faith was so great. But the trouble was real all the same, and so agonizing that even long afterward Alyosha thought of that sorrowful day as one of the bitterest, most fateful days of his life. If someone were to ask, "Could all his grief and turmoil really have come down to nothing more than his elder's body showing signs of premature decay instead of performing miracles on the spot?" I have to answer plainly, without dancing around it: "Yes, that's exactly what it was." I'd only ask the reader not to be too quick to laugh at my young hero's pure heart. I'm not trying to excuse him, or justify his innocent faith on the grounds of his youth, or how little schooling he'd had, or anything of that kind. I want to state, on the contrary, that I have genuine respect for the qualities of his heart. No doubt a young man who took in impressions cautiously, whose love ran lukewarm, whose mind was more prudent than suited his age and so worth little, might well have avoided what happened to my hero—I grant that. But in some cases it's actually more to a person's credit to be swept away by a feeling, however unreasonable, that springs from a great love, than to remain unmoved. And this is even truer in youth, since a young man who's always sensible is a young man to be suspected, and worth little—that's my opinion!
"But," reasonable people will perhaps object, "not every young man can believe in such a superstition, and your hero is no model for the rest."
To which I answer again: "Yes! my hero had faith, a faith both holy and steadfast, but I'm still not going to apologize for him."

Although I said above, perhaps too hastily, that I wouldn't explain or justify my hero, I can see that some explanation is needed if the rest of my story is to make sense. Let me say, then, that it wasn't really a matter of miracles. There was no frivolous, impatient hankering for miracles in his mind. And Alyosha needed no miracles at that moment, no triumphant confirmation of some preconceived notion—oh, no, not at all—what he saw before everything else was one figure: the figure of his beloved elder, the figure of that holy man he revered with such adoration. The fact is that all the love hidden away in his pure young heart, love for everyone and everything, had over the past year become concentrated—perhaps wrongly so—on a single being, his beloved elder. That being had, for so long, been accepted by him as his ideal, that all his youthful strength and energy could hardly help but turn toward that ideal, to the point of forgetting, in the moment, "everyone and everything else." He remembered afterward how, on that terrible day, he'd completely forgotten his brother Dmitri, about whom he'd been so anxious and troubled just the day before; he'd forgotten, too, to bring the two hundred roubles to Ilusha's father, though he'd meant so warmly to do it the evening before. But again, it wasn't miracles he needed, only "the higher justice," which he believed had been violated by the blow that had so suddenly and cruelly wounded his heart. And what does it matter that this "justice" Alyosha was seeking inevitably took the shape, in his mind, of miracles that ought to be worked immediately by the ashes of his beloved teacher? After all, everyone in the monastery cherished the same thought, the same hope—even those whose minds Alyosha revered, Father Païssy himself, for instance. And so Alyosha, untroubled by doubt, gave his own dreams the same shape as everyone else's. A whole year of monastery life had settled this expectation into a habit in his heart. But it was justice, justice, he thirsted for—not simply miracles.

And now the man who, he believed, should have been exalted above everyone in the whole world—that man, instead of receiving the glory owed to him, had suddenly been brought low and dishonored! What for? Who had judged him? Who could have decreed such a thing? Those were the questions that tore at his inexperienced, untested heart. He couldn't bear, without humiliation, without something like resentment even, that the holiest of holy men should be exposed to the jeering, spiteful mockery of a frivolous crowd so far beneath him. Even setting miracles aside, even if there'd been nothing marvelous to justify his hopes, why this indignity, why this humiliation, why this premature decay, "beyond nature," as the spiteful monks put it? Why this "sign from heaven," which they proclaimed so triumphantly alongside Father Ferapont, and what gave them the right, as they believed, to proclaim it? Where was the hand of Providence? Why had Providence hidden its face "at the most critical moment," as Alyosha saw it, as though willingly submitting itself to the blind, mute, pitiless laws of nature?

That was why Alyosha's heart was bleeding, and, as I've already said, the sting of it all was that the man he loved more than anything on earth should be shamed and humiliated! This murmuring against fate may have been shallow and unreasonable in my hero, but I repeat, for the third time—and I'm ready to admit it may be hard to defend the feeling—I'm glad my hero didn't show himself too reasonable in that moment, since any sensible man will always come back around to reason in time; but if love doesn't get the upper hand in a boy's heart at such an extraordinary moment, when will it? I won't, however, pass over something strange that surfaced for a while in Alyosha's mind at this fateful, murky moment. This new element was the disturbing impression left by his conversation with Ivan, which now clung persistently to Alyosha's mind. It haunted him just then. Oh, it wasn't that anything fundamental, elemental, so to speak, in his soul's faith had been shaken. He loved his God and believed in Him steadfastly, even as he suddenly found himself murmuring against Him. And yet a vague but tormenting, unsettling impression left by his talk with Ivan the day before suddenly revived in his soul, seeming to force its way up to the surface of his awareness.

It had begun to grow dark when Rakitin, cutting across the pine grove from the hermitage toward the monastery, suddenly spotted Alyosha lying face down on the ground under a tree, motionless, apparently asleep. He went over and called him by name.
"You, here, Alexey? Can you really have—" he began, wondering, then broke off. He'd meant to say, "Can you really have sunk to this?"
Alyosha didn't look at him, but from a slight movement Rakitin could tell at once that he'd heard and understood.
"What's the matter?" he went on; but the surprise on his face gradually gave way to a smile that grew more and more ironic.
"I say, I've been looking for you the last two hours. You just vanished. What are you doing? What's this foolishness? You might at least look at me...."

Alyosha lifted his head, sat up, and leaned his back against the tree. He wasn't crying, but there was suffering and irritation in his face. Still, he didn't look at Rakitin—he looked off to one side, past him.
"You know your face has changed completely? None of your famous mildness left in it at all. Angry with someone? Has someone been mistreating you?"
"Leave me alone," Alyosha said suddenly, with a tired wave of his hand, still looking away.

"Oho! So that's how it is with us! So you can snap at people like an ordinary mortal, can you. That's a bit of a fall from the angels. I say, Alyosha, you've surprised me, do you hear? I mean it. It's been a long time since anything around here surprised me. I always took you for an educated man...."
Alyosha looked at him at last, but vaguely, as though barely taking in what he was saying.

"Can you really be so upset simply because your old man's started to stink? You don't mean to tell me you seriously believed he was going to work miracles?" Rakitin exclaimed, genuinely surprised again.
"I believed it, I believe it, I want to believe it, and I will believe it—what more do you want?" Alyosha cried, irritated.

"Nothing at all, my boy. Damn it all, no schoolboy of thirteen believes in that sort of thing nowadays. But there you have it.... So now you're furious at your God, rebelling against Him—He hasn't handed out the promotion, hasn't pinned on the medal! Well, aren't you all a fine bunch!"
Alyosha stared at Rakitin a long while, his eyes half closed, and something suddenly flashed in them... but not anger at Rakitin.
"I'm not rebelling against my God—I simply 'don't accept His world.'" Alyosha suddenly gave a strained smile.
"What do you mean, you don't accept the world?" Rakitin thought over the answer for a moment. "What kind of idiocy is that?"
Alyosha didn't answer.
"Come on, enough of this nonsense, down to business. Have you eaten anything today?"
"I don't remember.... I think I have."

"You need feeding up, to judge by your face. It's enough to make a person sorry just looking at you. You didn't sleep all night either, I hear, you had some sort of gathering in there. And then all this uproar afterward. Most likely you've had nothing but a mouthful of holy bread. I've got some sausage in my pocket, brought it from town just in case, though you won't touch sausage, I suppose...."
"Give me some."

"Well, I never! You're really going for it! It's a regular mutiny, barricades and all! All right, my boy, we'd better make the most of it. Come to my place.... I could use a drop of vodka myself, I'm dead tired. Vodka's probably too much for you, I'd guess... or would you like some of that too?"
"Give me some vodka too."
"Well now! You do surprise me, brother!" Rakitin looked at him in amazement. "All right, either way, vodka or sausage, this is a fine bit of luck and shouldn't go to waste. Come along."
Alyosha got up without a word and followed Rakitin.
"If your little brother Ivan could see this, wouldn't he be surprised! By the way, your brother Ivan set off for Moscow this morning, did you know?"

"Yes," Alyosha answered listlessly, and suddenly the image of his brother Dmitri rose before his mind. But only for a moment, and although it reminded him of something that couldn't be put off, some duty, some terrible obligation, even that reminder left no real mark on him, didn't reach his heart, and instantly faded from his mind and was forgotten. But, long afterward, Alyosha remembered this.

"Your brother Ivan once said I was a 'liberal fool with no talent whatsoever.' You yourself once couldn't resist letting me know I was 'dishonorable.' Well! I'd like to see what your talent and your sense of honor do for you now." Rakitin finished this thought to himself, in a whisper.

"Listen!" he said aloud, "let's take the path beyond the monastery, straight to town. Hm! I ought to stop by Madame Hohlakov's on the way, by the by. Just imagine, I wrote and told her everything that happened, and would you believe it, she wrote straight back in pencil—the lady has a passion for writing notes—that 'she would never have expected such conduct from a man of such a reverend character as Father Zossima.' Those were her very words: 'conduct.' She's angry too. Eh, what a bunch you all are! Wait!" he suddenly cried again. He stopped abruptly, and, taking Alyosha by the shoulder, made him stop too.

"Do you know, Alyosha," he peered inquisitively into his eyes, caught up in some sudden new thought that had just struck him, and though he was laughing on the outside, he plainly felt uneasy about saying the new idea out loud, so hard did he still find it to believe in the strange, unexpected mood he now saw in Alyosha. "Alyosha, do you know where we'd better go?" he finally brought out, timidly and with a sly edge.
"I don't care... wherever you like."
"Let's go to Grushenka's, eh? Will you come?" Rakitin finally got out, trembling with nervous suspense.
"Let's go to Grushenka's," Alyosha answered calmly, at once, and this quick, calm agreement caught Rakitin so off guard that he nearly jumped back.
"Well! Would you look at that!" he cried in amazement, but grabbing Alyosha firmly by the arm, he led him off down the path, still afraid he might change his mind.
They walked along in silence; Rakitin was genuinely afraid to talk.

"And how glad she'll be, how delighted!" he muttered, then fell silent again. And in truth it wasn't to please Grushenka that he was bringing Alyosha to her. He was a practical man and never undertook anything without some prospect of gain for himself. His purpose here was twofold: first, a vengeful wish to witness "the downfall of the righteous," Alyosha's fall "from saint to sinner," which he was already savoring in his imagination; and second, he had his eye on a certain material gain for himself, of which more will be said later.
"So the critical moment has arrived," he thought to himself with spiteful glee, "and we'll catch it right as it happens, since that's exactly what we're after."
